items.title: Stack, naming and format foundations
items.context: Settled with the developer on 2026-11-02 while building Phase 1.
items.decision: CLI is `dsheets` (name kept in internal/brand). Go; any web UI is served on localhost by the Go binary (`dsheets serve`) as plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step or framework. All sheet numbers are CEL doubles. Range keys such as `[18..35]` live in lookup data. Evidence is shown by default. Wording is domain- and org-neutral: 'target', never 'partner'; generic examples such as specs/order-checkout.
items.rationale: Developer's choices from the original handoff's open questions; the tool should read as usable within a team or across organisations. Don't re-ask these.

items.title: Cross-team model: one repository per team, a registry, follow main
items.context: Agreed and built 2026-11-03 (PR #1). Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-03-cross-repo-references-design.md; docs/repositories.md, docs/flows.md.
items.decision: Each team keeps its sheets and interfaces in its own repository; cross-team references (`alias:path`) are read-only and follow the default branch. A registry repository of git submodules lists the teams. `dsheets impact` tells a producing team, in its own pull request, which other teams' flows its change breaks. Only each team's sheets folder is fetched, shallow and sparse. Whether a failing check blocks a merge is the organisation's CI policy, not dsheets'.
items.rationale: Teams change signatures without meetings, assuming nobody consumes them; producers must learn what they break before merging.

items.title: Visual editor design
items.context: Agreed in conversation 2026-11-03; spec docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-03-visual-editor-design.md (mockups in the git-ignored .superpowers/brainstorm). Refines the 2026-11-02 call that slicing is done in flow.toml rather than by drag-and-drop: the flow panel now pins rows with form actions ('compute here'), still not drag-and-drop.
items.decision: One editor for everyone, turned on with `dsheets serve --edit`; edits happen on the existing sheet and flow pages through a side panel with live preview. Saves write only the changed TOML spans, keep comments and formatting byte-for-byte elsewhere, and are refused only for errors the edit introduces. Files reached through alias: are read-only. Out of scope for now: creating sheets or flows from scratch, CSV and case editing, renaming after first save, git operations, re-slicing flows on save.
items.rationale: Product managers should not edit TOML, and developers must find the editor faster than the TOML, not a simplified tool.

items.title: Build the visual editor next, starting with the TOML writer
items.context: Concierge session 2026-11-06. Alternatives weighed: PR diffs first (T-5: smaller, useful in reviews straight away; BACKLOG.md's suggested order put it first, but that was written an hour before the editor design was agreed); lists design first (T-8: the only open format question; T-1 is format-agnostic, so it can wait).
items.decision: Build the visual editor in four milestones (T-1 to T-4), starting with the comment-preserving TOML writer and file store (T-1), preceded by the editor's implementation plan. PR diffs (T-5) and the change-to-work project (T-6) follow the editor.
items.rationale: The design is agreed and only needs a plan; the editor is the point of Phase 2 (product managers authoring without TOML); the writer is the riskiest part and testable on its own; it can also back the formatter (T-7); and the spec sequences T-6 and PR diffs after the editor because they share one comparison.

items.title: Where the backlog lives
items.context: Hopback was added 2026-11-06 while the backlog lived in BACKLOG.md, which README links to in a public repository.
items.decision: Hopback holds the working backlog (status, ranks, decisions). BACKLOG.md stays as the public roadmap and is refreshed at milestones, not on every change.
items.rationale: One place for agents to track work across sessions, without breaking the public roadmap README points to.
